HISTORICAL NOTICE. 



The Meditations of S. Anselm were his own com- 
munings with God, in which he poured out his heart 
before Him. His disciple Eadmer, the compa- 
panion of his toils and of his exile, says of them ; 
" What a of his vigils ? The whole day most often 
did not suffice for giving counsel ; the greater part 
of the night was wont to be added to this end. 
Moreover by night he corrected books, which up 
to that time had throughout the world been most 
corrupt ; he gave himself continuously to holy medi- 
tations, and from the contemplation of tlie sovereign 
bliss and longing for life eternal, he poured forth 
showers of tears. He wept most bitterly the mi- 
series of this life and his own sins, (whatever he 
may have had,) and the sins of others, and scarcely 
took a little sleep before the night- vigils and often 
none." 

Of the Prayers, on the contrary, Eadmer speaks 
generally, as having been written and published in 
compliance with the desire of friends. S. Anselm 
himself mentions four prayers, and four only, as 
having been written at the request of others.** 

S. Anselm*s life is commonly divided into five pe- 
riods. In his twenty-seventh year (A. D. 1060) he

entered the Monastery of Bee; at thirty he succeeded 
Lanfranc as Prior ; at forty-five he became Abbot. Af- 
ter fifteen other years, (A.D. 1093) he was at sixty 
nominated Arch-Bishop of Canterbury by William 
Rufus. After sixteen years more of labour and toil 
he slept in peace. 

The second, third, and eighteenth of his Meditations, 
at all events, and many of his Prayers were written 
before he was Abbot. His eighteenth Meditation and 
nine certainly of his Prayers were employed before 
A.D. 1075 by abbot John.<^ It is noticed that neither 
in the Epistle of Durandus, in which he acknowledges 
the present (as it would seem) of the second and third 
Meditations, nor in S. Anselm*s answer,^ is there any 
mention of any dignity of S.Anselm. Anselm also 
salutes the Abbot Durandus, as a father. The whole 
picture of S. Anselm's early piety makes it seem to 
me probable, that the deviations, spoken of in the 
third Meditation, were spiritual only, unless indeed 
this Meditation was, like some of the Prayers, written 
for another. Before he was fifteen, he, born of noble 
and wealthy parents, revolved how he might best live 
after the will of God, and he conceived, that no mode 
of life was better than that of monks. He even prayed 
for sickness, that so he might obtain what he longed for 
as a means of serving God. His wish being deferred, 
he still purposed through the grace of God, to do what 
was then denied him. His fervour afterwards, for a 
time, somewhat chilled ; he became idle, ** preferring 
youthful games to the study of letters, in which he had 
practised himself exceedingly." Still the utmost spo- 
ken of is a degree of secularity. When he left his 
father's house, he did so in the society of a Clerk. 
When became to Bee, he attached himself at once to 
Lanfranc. Soon he became more intimate with him 
than his other disciples, and was engaged day and

night in study. He wore his frame with vigils, cold, 
and meagreness of food, so that he thought that he 
underwent the privations of the monastic life without 
its rewards. The account of Eadmer describes an easy 
transition from a secular to a monastic life, not a con- 
version from Satan to God. 

The praise of Durandus, Abbot of Casa Dei, shews 
how S. Anselm's Meditations were esteemed in his 
own time. He speaks of them to S. Anselm, as " ut- 
tered and written most piously out of thy contrite spirit 
and out of the piety of thy contrite heart. We read 
therein thy piou$ tears, and pour forth our own, mar- 
velling at the abundant dew of blessing which over- 
streams thy heart, and how a stream therefrom sinks, 
without a murmur, into our hearts. For so in truth 
it is. The piety of thy written prayer awakens in us 
the piety of the slumbering compunction ; so that, 
bounding forth as it were, in mind, we rejoice with thee, 
loving these things in thee, or rather thee in them, and 
above them and through them, loving God in thee. " 

As S. Anselm was towards God, so he was towards 
man, " Fearing, " he answers, " not only lest your 
love should benefit me little or nothing, because I am 
not what you love, but also lest my own lukewarm- 
ness which you know not in me, should injure me 
exceedingly, I pray, implore you, not to think of 
me or love me, as though I had already made any 
spiritual prc^ess ; but to this end love me, and, lov- 
ing, pray that I may. For so will both your esteem 
of me, and your love towards me be true, and my ex- 
ultation in your love be without fear." 

Mention is made of his Meditations as a whole, 
in the Soliloquy® of Card. Bonaventura, about 150 
years after his decease. 

The Prayers of S. Anselm were collected, some 
from several MSS., some from a single but ancient MS.

John, Abbot of Fescam en Eaux, inserted (as was said 
above) nine, at least, of them, in a manual of devo- 
tion which he compiled between A.D. 1066 and 1075 
for the use and at the request of Agnes, daughter of 
William Count of Poitiers, and widow of the Emperor 
Henry III. Abbot John, although much older than 
S. Anselm, speaks so distinctly and repeatedly of his 
own work as a compilation only, that tiere can be no 
doubt that the prayers are not his own, but inserted 
by him from his younger contemporary S. Anselm, 
who was, at this time (from A.D. 1063 to 1078) Prior 
of the neighbouring monastery of Bee. 

.An extract from the Preface will shew the value 
which Abbot John attached to the devotional writings 
which he brought together, and so, among them, to 
many Prayers of S. Anselm. 

"'You were pleased, Lady Empress, long since to 
ask me to collect for you from the Scriptures, some 
brief and full discourses, wherein, according to the 
law of your order, you might, without over-much 
toil, learn the rule of holy living. For every degree, 
age, and sex, has in holy Scripture teaching suitable 
to itself, for the formation of its life ; so that each, 
walking aright in that calling wherein he hath been 
called, may attain to that Kingdom where are many 
mansions. — Knowing then the pious longings of your 
heart, I took pains, and quickly culled from the 
writings of the fathers certain passages, that you might 
have with you every where truthful teaching, which 
may more fully shew you the way whereby a faith- 
ful widow should walk righteously and holily." — 
"Although I think that what my poor" self has culled 
may suffice for your salvation, yet since from the 
account of friends, I have learnt that you long and ask 
that the little book which I have published, on the

contemplation of God and the love of Christ, and on 
that Jerusalem above, the mother of all the faithful, 
should be written to you, my heart, I own, rejoices 
greatly, and magnifies in you God die Giver of all 
good. — Receive then, good soul, excellent ensample 
of holy widowhood, with an ever watchful heart, the 
little work you ask for, which, by the grace of Christ, 
I have culled, wherein you will fiiid, in great measure, 
sweet words of heavenly contemplation, which are to 
be read reverently and to be meditated on with due 
fear, lest any coming lukewarm and undevout be con-

is especially due to those who allow not their minds 
to be overshadowed by carnal longings and earthly 
desires. But when read with tears and deep devotion,

MEDITATION I. 



OF THE DIGNITY AND MISERY OF MAN S 
CONDITION. 



Awake, O my soul, awake ; put forth thy spirit ; 
arouse thy feeling ; drive from thee the sluggishness 
of thy deadly lethargy, take up to thee anxiety for 
thy salvation. Be the wanderings of vain thoughts 
put to flight, let idleness depart, he diligence main- 
tained. Give thyself to holy meditation, cling thou 
to the good things of God. Leave the things of 
time, and give thyself to the things of eternity. 
What then more useful, what more healthful, in so 
heavenly an employment of thy mind, wilt thou be 
able to think on, than in sweetest meditation to re- 
collect the immeasurable kindnesses of thy Creator ? 
Consider then even in the very beginning of His 
Creation, how great excellence, how great dignity

My life frighteneth me, because that when diligently 
examined, it seemeth to me almost entirely either sin 
or barrenness : and if there do appear any fruit in 
it, it is either so unreal, or so imperfect, or in some 
way or other so corrupt, that it cannot but either 
displease or at all events fail to please God. 

Well then, O sinner, thy life, I say not almost 
all, but really all, is either in sin, and so, damnable, 
or unfruitful, and so, contemptible. But why do I 
separate the unfruitful from the damnable ? Verily 
if it is unfruitful, it is also damnable. For that is 
clear and true which the Truth hath said, " Every 
tree which bringeth not forth good fruit, shall be 
hewn down and cast into the fire."*
